The PDF holds the 9-page article plus a Science Advances information page (p. 10). The Supplementary Materials are not in this PDF.
source.title_on_document: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content

supplement.where: A separate Supplementary Materials file listed on p. 8 ('This PDF file includes: Sections S1 to S9 Tables S1 to S18 Figs. S1 to S6'). The document gives no direct URL for it; the article is online at https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adn5290 (p. 10).
supplement.holds: As cited in the main text: section S1 (all study questions), S3 (evidence that Human-only writers did not use AI), S4 (preregistered test of Human-only against the combined AI conditions), S5 (exploratory ownership, profit, and ethics outcomes), S6 (example stories), S7 and S8 (interface screenshots and exact item wording), S9 (preregistration copy); tables S1 and S2 (balance), S3 (cited after the first novelty result), S4 (robustness with fixed effects), S5 and S7 (writer self-assessments), S6 (emotional characteristics), S8 (AI access by DAT), S9 and S10 (DAT interactions), S11 (similarity to other stories in the condition); figs. S1 (violin plot of raw data) and S2 (remaining DAT graphs). The main text prints no standard errors and no outcome SDs. It prints only two arm means: the one-idea usefulness mean of 5.21 (p. 3) and the Human-only mean similarity to a GPT-4 idea of 82.85 (p. 5). Tables S12 to S18 and figs. S3 to S6 are not cited in the main text.

paper_design_summary: In a preregistered online experiment on Prolific (UK), writers were randomly assigned to write an eight-sentence story with no AI (Human-only), with the option to request one three-sentence GPT-4 story idea, or with the option to request up to five such ideas, and 293 writers were analyzed. A separate group of 600 Prolific evaluators rated six stories each on novelty, usefulness, and emotional characteristics before being told the writers' conditions (3519 evaluations remain). The authors also computed the embedding cosine similarity of each story to the other stories in its condition and to a GPT-4 idea.

studies.label: Writer experiment (short-story writing with optional GPT-4 story ideas), rated by a separate evaluator sample

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing condition: Human-only (no mention of or access to generative AI), Human with one GenAI idea (option to request one three-sentence GPT-4 story idea), or Human with five GenAI ideas (option to request up to five). Story topic (open seas, jungle, different planet) was also randomized. The paper calls its analysis intention-to-treat because AI-arm writers who requested no idea stay in their assigned arm (p. 6). It does not keep everyone assigned: 3 Human-only writers who admitted using AI were dropped, and so were non-completers, some of whom had written stories (p. 7).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomized into one of three experimental conditions: Human-only, Human with one GenAI idea, and Human with five GenAI ideas.
assignment.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', third paragraph; also p. 2, Fig. 1 caption, and p. 2, Introduction text above the Results heading (left column)
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 8, 'Preregistration and ethics approval': AsPredicted.org (ID 136723); copy in section S9 (not in this PDF)

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Writers wrote the story with no mention of or access to generative AI (p. 2). Three writers in this arm who admitted using generative AI were dropped per the preregistration (p. 7). The arm's analyzed count is not printed.

arms.name: Human with one GenAI idea
arms.description: Option to click 'Generate Story Idea…' once and receive a three-sentence GPT-4 story idea; no copy and paste (p. 7). 82 of the 100 analyzed writers requested it (p. 2).

arms.name: Human with five GenAI ideas
arms.description: Option to request up to five three-sentence GPT-4 story ideas, each visible to the writer; no copy and paste (p. 7). 93 of the 98 analyzed writers requested at least one, 2.55 requests on average, and 24.5 percent requested all five (p. 2).

participants.exclusions: Of 500 Prolific participants who began the writer study, 169 exited before giving consent, 22 were dropped for not giving consent, 13 dropped out before completing, and 3 Human-only writers who admitted using generative AI were dropped per the preregistration, which leaves 293 analyzed writers and stories (p. 7). Assignment came after consent and the DAT (Fig. 1 caption, p. 2), so the 3 dropped Human-only writers had been assigned. The evaluator-study text says that the evaluations of 'the writers who did not complete the writer study' were dropped (p. 7). This implies that some of the 13 non-completers had written a story and so had been assigned. The paper does not say how many, or in which arms. The number randomized is therefore not printed. It is at least 296 (293 analyzed plus the 3 dropped Human-only writers) and at most 309 (the participants who consented: 500 minus 169 minus 22; derived from p. 7). Analyzed counts by arm: 100 (one idea) and 98 (five ideas) (p. 2); the Human-only count is not printed. The DAT score was computed for 291 of the 293 analyzed writers (p. 3). Each evaluator was shown six stories (p. 7), and 3519 evaluations by 600 evaluators remain (p. 8), so 81 evaluations were dropped (derived: 5 evaluators kept four and 71 kept five). Evaluators were not assigned to AI.
participants.who: Writers: Prolific participants based in the United Kingdom with an approval rating of at least 95 percent from between 100 and 1,000,000 prior submissions, not selected on prior writing skills or creativity (p. 7). Evaluators: a separate set of 600 Prolific UK participants who had not taken part in the writer study and were not selected on publishing experience (pp. 2, 7).
participants.quote: Three participants in the Human-only condition admitted to using generative AI during their story writing exercise and—as per our preregistration—were therefore dropped from the analysis, resulting in a total number of writers and stories of 293.
participants.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', first paragraph; arm counts p. 2, Results, 'Baseline versus generative AI conditions', second paragraph; evaluators p. 2 and pp. 7-8

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 via OpenAI's GPT API
ai_tool.how_used: On request, the interface sent the fixed prompt 'Write a three-sentence summary of a story about [topic]' to GPT-4 and showed the reply (p. 7). Writers could not copy and paste the idea, customize the prompt, or interact with the model repeatedly (pp. 6-7). AI use was optional: 88.4 percent of the analyzed writers in the two AI arms requested at least one idea (p. 2). The paper's intention-to-treat analysis keeps AI-arm writers who requested no idea in their arm (p. 6), but assigned writers who admitted AI use or did not complete were dropped (p. 7).

task.description: Write a story of exactly eight sentences in English on a randomly assigned topic (an adventure on the open seas, in the jungle, or on a different planet), appropriate for a teenage and young adult audience (approximately 15 to 24 years of age); 'You can write about anything you like.' Automatic checks enforced the eight-sentence length (p. 7). Writers completed the Divergent Association Task first (p. 7). No financial incentives for performance or creativity (p. 1).

outcomes.name: Novelty index (evaluator-rated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean of three 9-point items (novel, original, rare) rated by Prolific evaluators before they were told the writers' conditions; Cronbach's alpha 0.92 (p. 8; Fig. 1 caption, p. 2). Preregistered index (p. 8). OLS on evaluations with condition dummies and robust SEs clustered by evaluator (p. 8). Results qualitatively unchanged with evaluator, story-order, and topic fixed effects and an indicator for accessing at least one AI idea (p. 3; table S4, not in this PDF). The three component items are coded separately as S1-O12 to S1-O14 (Fig. 2A, figure only).

outcomes.name: Similarity of each story to the other stories in its condition (embedding cosine similarity)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity x 100 (range 0 to 100) between the focal story's embedding and the average embedding of all other stories in the same condition; embeddings from OpenAI's embeddings API, model not named (pp. 4, 8). Higher means more similar, so the sign is reversed relative to diversity. In the Human-only condition the similarity scores span 8.10 points; the authors express the increases as 10.7 and 8.9 percent of that range (p. 4). Fig. 4A plots kernel densities by condition; Fig. 4B (top panel) plots the coefficients.

contrasts.reported: Human with one GenAI idea condition: b = 0.871, P < 0.001; 10.7% of the 8.10-point Human-only range (table S11 is cited for both arms). Positive b means more similar; direction coded for diversity (lower in treatment).
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Results, 'Similarity of stories', second paragraph; Fig. 4B top panel, p. 5; table S11 not in this PDF

contrasts.reported: Human with five GenAI ideas condition: b = 0.718, P = 0.003, see table S11; 8.9% of the 8.10-point Human-only range. Positive b means more similar; direction coded for diversity (lower in treatment).
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Results, 'Similarity of stories', second paragraph; Fig. 4B top panel, p. 5; table S11 not in this PDF

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity x 100 between each story's embedding and the average embedding of all other stories in its condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each output against the centroid (average embedding) of all other outputs in its own condition (leave-one-out centroid)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS of story-level similarity on condition dummies with robust standard errors (writer-study outcome, one story per writer; p. 8, 'Statistical analysis')
diversity_detail.notes: The paper reports similarity, not diversity: a positive coefficient means more homogeneous stories. Each story's score depends on the other stories in its own arm. Arm means and SDs are not printed in the main text; table S11 is not in this PDF.

company_involvement.description: No company staff among the authors (UCL School of Management; University of Exeter). Funding from the University of Exeter Business School and UCL School of Management; the authors declare no competing interests. GPT-4 was used through OpenAI's API as the study tool, with no stated OpenAI involvement.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, affiliations; p. 9, Acknowledgments (Funding; Competing interests)

eligibility.reason: Writers were randomized individually to Human-only or to the option of one or up to five GPT-4 story ideas (p. 7; Fig. 1 caption, p. 2). In all, 293 writers were analyzed (p. 7), 100 and 98 of them in the two AI arms (p. 2). The Human-only analyzed count and the number randomized are not printed, and criterion 2 is met by a wide margin. Stories were rated for novelty and usefulness by evaluators before they were told the conditions, and scored for embedding similarity to the other stories in their condition; the AI ideas were available while writing (pp. 2-4, 8). AI use was optional (88.4 percent of the analyzed AI-arm writers requested an idea, p. 2). The paper calls its analysis intention-to-treat because AI-arm writers who requested no idea stay in their arm (p. 6), but it does not keep everyone assigned: 3 Human-only writers who admitted using AI and an unstated number of non-completers were dropped after assignment (p. 7).

one_line_finding: Relative to Human-only, access to up to five GPT-4 story ideas raised evaluator-rated novelty by 8.1 percent (b = 0.311, P < 0.001) and usefulness by 9.0 percent (b = 0.453, P < 0.001) (p. 3, Fig. 2A), while stories in both AI arms were more similar to the other stories in their condition (one idea b = 0.871, P < 0.001; five ideas b = 0.718, P = 0.003) (p. 4; Fig. 4B, p. 5).
open_questions: The Human-only arm's analyzed count is not printed: 293 minus 100 minus 98 implies 95, left null because the paper does not state it.

The number randomized is not printed, overall or by arm. It is at least 296 (293 analyzed plus the 3 dropped Human-only writers) and at most 309 (those who consented, derived from p. 7). The evaluator-study sentence on p. 7 implies that some of the 13 non-completers had written stories and so had been assigned, but the paper does not say how many or in which arms.

The main text prints only coefficients, P values, percent changes, and two arm means. It points to tables S3, S4, S6, S11 and section S4 (the preregistered pooled test) for full results, and none of these is in this PDF. Whether those tables print standard errors, arm means, and SDs cannot be checked here. The six index components (S1-O12 to S1-O17) have no printed numbers.

Evaluator-rated outcomes are estimated on 3519 evaluations with SEs clustered by evaluator, not by writer (the unit of assignment). Under codebook section 10 these SEs may not qualify for pooling without a writer-level reanalysis (data and code are posted on Dryad).
The paper does not say whether the similarity outcomes were preregistered or primary; the preregistered indices it names are novelty and usefulness (p. 8).

Codebook rule 8.3 does not clearly separate the two AI arms: both supply fixed-prompt GPT-4 ideas and neither allows open chat, while the five-ideas arm allows more AI use. Review 1 should pick the primary contrast.

Construct coding of the exploratory items is a judgment call: well written (usefulness), surprising twist (novelty), and changed expectations (other; the paper motivates it with Jauss's idea of novel literature, so Review 1 could move it to novelty).

AI use was optional within the AI arms (82 of the 100 and 93 of the 98 analyzed writers requested ideas). The paper's intention-to-treat label covers take-up only: writers dropped after assignment (3 Human-only writers who admitted AI use and an unstated number of non-completers, p. 7) are not in the analysis.

The paper describes the random AI idea assigned to writers without one in two ways: 'within the same story topic' (p. 5) and 'from the same condition among all generative AI ideas' (p. 8). This affects only the anchoring measure (similarity to a GPT-4 idea), which is now reported in notes.

p. 2 says that the statistically significant differences in the preregistered indices come from the five-ideas arm, but p. 3 prints P = 0.021 (novelty) and P = 0.039 (usefulness) for the one-idea arm. The paper does not explain this, for example by a multiple-testing adjustment in the preregistration (section S9, not in this PDF).

Rule 7 cap: with the six Fig. 2A components listed, 16 outcomes qualify, so the anchoring measure (with_ai under the codebook rule) is left out and its numbers are in notes. Review 1 can restore it in place of another outcome.
notes: The PDF is the journal article (pp. 1-9) plus a Science Advances information page (p. 10); all supplementary sections, tables, and figures cited in the text are absent. Fig. 2 and Fig. 4B label their axes 'Effect size', but the plotted points match the raw b coefficients printed in the text (for example, novelty 0.207 and 0.311; similarity to other stories 0.871 and 0.718), so they show unstandardized coefficients with intervals. Heterogeneity by the writer's pre-treatment DAT score (mean 77.24, SD 6.48, computed for 291 of the 293 analyzed writers, p. 3): among low-DAT writers, one and five ideas raise novelty by 6.3 and 10.7 percent and usefulness by 5.5 and 11.5 percent; with five ideas, well written rises by up to 26.6 percent, enjoyment by up to 22.6 percent, and boring falls by up to 15.2 percent; little effect for high-DAT writers (p. 4, Fig. 3; tables S9 and S10 not in this PDF). Not listed as outcomes: evaluators' judgments of whether a story was written by AI, ownership and profit-split ratings after disclosure (ownership penalty of at least 25 percent, p. 6), and ethics attitudes (section S5); these are perceptions, not creativity scores. Also not listed (final pass): the similarity of each story to a GPT-4 story idea, a measure of anchoring on the AI idea. It is cosine similarity x 100 between the story embedding and the first idea the writer received or, for Human-only writers and AI-arm writers who requested none, a randomly assigned idea (pp. 5, 8). Relative to a Human-only mean of 82.85, stories were 5.2 percent more similar to the AI idea with one idea (b = 4.29, P < 0.001) and 5.0 percent with five ideas (b = 4.11, P < 0.001) (p. 5, left column; Fig. 4B bottom panel, p. 5). It is scored on stories written with AI available, so the codebook rule gives with_ai, construct other, measure embedding_similarity, unit output (293 stories). Listing the six Fig. 2A index components brings the qualifying outcomes to 16, above rule 7's cap of 15, and this measure is the least central of them: the paper uses it to explain the similarity result, and it scores neither creativity nor diversity across writers. Reconciliation: both screeners omitted the source.supplement block (they put the supplement facts in source.version), so the reconciler added it. Outcome IDs follow screener B's order (screener A had the anchoring outcome as S1-O4). Final pass: S1-O10 (anchoring) was removed and its numbers moved here; the six index components were added as S1-O12 to S1-O17; S1-O11 keeps its ID. The final pass also says the evaluators rated the stories before being told the conditions (the disclosure came after the ratings, Fig. 1 caption), and corrects source.supplement.holds, which had said that the main text prints no arm means. No other screened candidate reanalyzes these writers: c128 (Wan and Kalman) extends the design with its own participants (candidates.json).
